lists.title: Tagalog A1 Grammar Path
lists.description: First Tagalog: the ang/ng/sa marker system, actor-focus verbs with -um-, the na linker, the mga plural marker, may/wala existence and possession, and hindi negation.

lists.title: Tagalog A2 Grammar Path
lists.description: The focus system opens up: mag- beside -um-, the three aspects, object focus with -in and locative focus with -an, the ang/ng/sa pronoun sets, si and sina for names, questions with ba, and ma- adjectives with their linker.

lists.title: Tagalog B1 Grammar Path
lists.description: i- focus for things given and tools used, ma-/maka- for ability and the involuntary, the fixed order of the enclitic particles, ay inversion, comparison, the pseudo-verbs, may and mayroon, both number systems, and the three-way deictics.

lists.title: Tagalog B2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Causatives with magpa- and pa-...-in, the recent perfective that says 'just now', nominalisation with pag- and ka-...-an, relative clauses locked to focus, conditionals, reciprocal and social affixes, and pang- instruments.

lists.title: Tagalog C1 Grammar Path
lists.description: Register across formal Filipino, deep Tagalog and Taglish; focus choice as information structure; and the aspect particles na and pa that the verb form alone cannot carry.

lists.title: Tagalog C2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Literary Filipino and its older particles, affixed words that have drifted from their roots, and code-switching as a rule-governed system rather than a lapse.

points.title: The ang phrase marks the sentence's topic
points.function: Identify what the sentence is 'about'
points.explanation: Tagalog doesn't have a fixed "subject" the way English does. Instead, one noun phrase — marked by ang — is the TOPIC: the participant the sentence is "about," chosen by which role the verb's affix highlights. Kumain ang bata ("The child ate") marks the eater (bata) as topic because kumain is an actor-focus verb.

drills.hint: topic marker; kumain is actor-focus, so the eater is what the sentence is about
the marker that puts the drinker in the topic slot, since the verb highlights the actor
the marker on the phrase the sentence is about; pumunta is actor-focus, so the goer holds that role
the topic marker; pumunta is actor-focus, so the goer takes it, and a question does not change that

drills.translation: The dog didn't eat this morning.
drills.hint: hindi negates the verb but leaves the marking alone; the eater is still what the sentence is about
the topic marker itself has no plural; it goes in front of the plural word, not after it
no verb here: the job word is the predicate, and the topic marker introduces who is being described

points.title: ng marks a non-topic actor, object, or possessor
points.function: Mark a noun that isn't the topic
points.explanation: ng (pronounced "nang") marks a noun phrase that ISN'T the topic — often the object when the actor is topic, or a possessor: Kumain ang bata ng pagkain ("The child ate [some] food") marks pagkain with ng because it's the object, not the topic. The same ng also shows possession: bahay ng kaibigan ("friend's house").

drills.hint: non-topic marker on the thing acted on; the child already holds the topic slot
possessor marker: the owner of the house, which is not the topic of anything here
the marker that ties a thing to its owner, with the owner following the thing owned
the verb puts the bread in the topic slot, so the eater has to be marked as a non-topic actor
the drinker is the topic, so the milk takes the marker for a thing acted on
you are the topic of the buying, so the bread gets the non-topic marker; questions use the same one

drills.translation: The car key is on the table.
drills.hint: the possessor marker works for things as well as people: the key belongs to the car

points.title: sa marks location, direction, or a specific place
points.function: Say where something happens
points.explanation: sa introduces location or direction — "in," "at," "to": Pumunta ang bata sa bahay ("The child went to the house"). It's also used for definite/specific places and times.

drills.translation: The child went to the house.
drills.hint: the marker for where the motion is headed

drills.translation: The man drank at the house.
drills.hint: the marker for the place the drinking happened, not for the thing drunk
the marker that puts the eating in a place

drills.translation: Are you going to the market?
drills.hint: the marker for the place the going is aimed at; a question takes the same one
the same marker also introduces a definite time, not only a place

drills.translation: The dog ran in the park.
drills.hint: the marker for where the running happened

drills.translation: The children went into the school.
drills.hint: the marker before the place they moved into; it does not change for a plural topic

points.title: Actor-focus verbs with the -um- infix
points.function: Build actor-focus verbs from a root
points.explanation: Many Tagalog action verbs form their actor-focus version by inserting -um- right after the root's first consonant: kain ("eat") → kumain; bili ("buy") → bumili. If the root starts with a vowel, -um- simply attaches to the front instead: inom ("drink") → uminom.

drills.hint: ate: the root is kain, and the actor-focus infix goes in right after its first consonant
drank: built on the root inom, which opens with a vowel, so the actor-focus infix has no consonant to sit behind and attaches at the front
bought: the root is bili, taking the actor-focus infix behind its first consonant
left, went away: built on the root alis, which opens with a vowel, so the actor-focus infix has no consonant to sit behind and rides in front instead

drills.translation: The child didn't go to school yesterday.
drills.hint: went in, attended: the root is pasok, with the actor-focus infix after its first consonant; hindi never alters the verb itself

drills.translation: Did you ride a jeep earlier?
drills.hint: rode, got on: the root is sakay, and the actor-focus infix goes in after its first consonant; ba leaves the verb alone
called, phoned: the root is tawag, taking the actor-focus infix behind its first consonant

points.title: The linker na
points.function: Connect a describing word to what it describes
points.explanation: na links a describing word to what it describes, in either order — noun + na + adjective: bata na mabuti ("a good child"). In fast speech na often shortens to -ng and attaches to the previous word if it ends in a vowel (batang mabuti), but na is the safe default to write.

drills.hint: the standalone spelling of the linker between the noun and the adjective after it — written as its own word here, not fused onto the noun
the full form of the linker that ties the house to its size, rather than the shortened suffix
the linker that joins the description to the person it describes

drills.translation: My mother is a kind teacher.
drills.hint: the linker between a quality and the person it describes, here with the quality first; the word before the gap ends in a consonant, so the shortened suffix is not available
the describing word and the thing described need the linker between them, in its full standalone shape
negation does not touch the join between a quality and its noun; the linker still belongs there in full

drills.sentence: Gusto mo ba ng mainit {{answer}} kape?
drills.hint: the join between the temperature word and the drink; a question leaves it exactly as a statement would have it

points.title: mga marks the plural
points.function: Make a noun plural
points.explanation: Tagalog nouns don't change form for plural — instead, the particle mga (pronounced "mah-NGA") goes right before the noun: bata ("child") → mga bata ("children"); bahay ("house") → mga bahay ("houses").

drills.hint: the plural particle that goes before the noun
the same particle again: the noun itself keeps one single shape for both numbers
the particle that makes a noun plural without altering the noun
the plural particle slots between the topic marker and the noun
more than one fruit; the plural particle follows the non-topic marker and precedes the noun
more than one key: the plural particle sits directly in front of the noun in a question as well

drills.translation: There are children in the park.
drills.hint: several of them exist; the plural particle comes right before the noun it counts

points.title: Existence and possession: may and wala
points.function: Say that something exists, or that you have it
points.explanation: may states that something exists or that someone has something: May pagkain ako, literally "there-is food I," means "I have food." Its negative wala works a little differently — it needs the linker -ng on the pronoun: Wala akong pagkain ("I have no food"), not "wala pagkain ako."

drills.hint: the existential particle that opens a possession statement; the possessor pronoun comes after the thing possessed
the affirmative existence marker, with a plural possessor pronoun at the end
the negative counterpart of that existential particle; the pronoun after it takes the -ng linker (akong, not ako)
the existence word that opens even a yes/no question, standing before the thing owned
the same particle with no owner named at all, stating only that something exists
the negated existential, with a third-person pronoun carrying the linker after it
the negative existential again, here with the exclusive 'we' and its linker

points.title: hindi negates verbs and adjectives
points.function: Say what isn't true or didn't happen
points.explanation: hindi is the general negator for verbs and adjectives — placed right before what it negates: Hindi kumain ang bata ("The child didn't eat"), Hindi malaki ang bahay ("The house isn't big").

drills.hint: the general negator, sitting immediately in front of the verb it cancels
the negator, here cancelling a size adjective rather than a verb
the one negator that covers verbs and adjectives alike; it comes first, before the predicate
the negator for a not-yet-begun action, with the actor pronoun tucked in after it
the negator at the head of a yes/no question, ahead of the pronoun and the question particle
the negator before an ongoing/habitual verb, with the actor pronoun in between
the negator directly in front of the adjective; the place phrase stays at the end

points.title: mag- actor-focus verbs, beside -um-
points.function: Use the other actor-focus prefix, and hear the difference
points.explanation: mag- is the second big actor-focus affix: magluto 'cook', magbasa 'read', maglinis 'clean'. Many roots take both -um- and mag- with a real difference: bumili 'buy (for oneself)' vs magbili 'sell'; umalis 'leave' vs mag-alis 'remove something'. Broadly -um- leans toward the actor experiencing the action and mag- toward the actor doing something deliberate or repeated — but the pairs are learned word by word.

drills.hint: mag- + luto, completed aspect
-um- + bili — buying for oneself

drills.translation: I clean the house every Saturday.
drills.hint: mag- + linis, incompleted

drills.translation: The child played at the park.
drills.hint: mag- + laro
root alis + -um-, completed; with mag- this same root would mean taking something away instead of departing
root aral + mag-, contemplated; a hyphen separates the prefix from the vowel-initial root, whose first syllable doubles
root trabaho + mag-, completed; negation leaves the aspect form untouched

points.title: Aspect: completed, incompleted, contemplated
points.function: Mark when the action stands, not when it happened
points.explanation: Tagalog verbs mark ASPECT, not tense. Three forms: completed (begun and finished — kumain, nagluto), incompleted (begun, still going — kumakain, nagluluto), contemplated (not yet begun — kakain, magluluto). For -um- verbs the incompleted and contemplated reduplicate the first syllable of the root; for mag- verbs the prefix becomes nag-/nagCV-/magCV-. The same form covers English past and present perfect.

drills.hint: -um- completed
-um- incompleted — reduplicated
-um- contemplated
mag- completed → nag-
root hintay + mag-, incompleted; the first syllable of the root doubles for an action still under way
root inom + -um-, incompleted; the root opens with a vowel, so the affix goes in front and the root's first syllable doubles

points.title: Object focus with -in
points.function: Make the thing acted on the topic
points.explanation: When the OBJECT is the topic, the verb takes -in and the object gets ang: Kinain ko ang mansanas 'I ate the apple' — literally 'the apple was eaten by me'. The actor moves to a ng pronoun (ko, mo, niya). Object focus is the normal choice when the object is definite, which is far more often than English passive would be used.

drills.hint: kain + -in, completed aspect
basa + -in, completed aspect
sara + -in, completed
linis + -in, contemplated
gawa + -in, incompleted aspect
luto + -in, the bare command form with the suffix intact

drills.sentence: Hindi ko {{answer}} ang kwarto ko kahapon.
drills.translation: I didn't tidy my room yesterday.
drills.hint: ayos + -in, completed; the root starts with a vowel, so the completed marker sits in front rather than inside

points.title: Locative focus with -an
points.function: Make the place or recipient the topic
points.explanation: -an puts the LOCATION, direction, or recipient in topic position: Binilhan ko ang tindahan 'I bought from the store'; Pinuntahan namin ang museo 'We went to the museum'. Compare with -in, which makes the thing itself the topic. Choosing the focus is choosing what the sentence is about.

drills.hint: bili + -an — the store is the topic
punta + -an — the destination

drills.translation: She gave the child a gift.
drills.hint: bigay + -an — the recipient
linis + -an — the surface

drills.sentence: {{answer}} ng guro ang mga bata tuwing Lunes.
drills.translation: The teacher teaches the children every Monday.
drills.hint: turo + -an, incompleted; the learners are the topic, and the root's last vowel raises before the suffix
drills.gloss: ___ · GEN · teacher · NOM · PL · child · every · Monday

drills.sentence: {{answer}} mo ba ang nanay mo kahapon?
drills.translation: Did you help your mother yesterday?
drills.hint: tulong + -an, completed; the person helped is the topic, and the root's last vowel raises before the suffix

points.title: ang pronouns
points.function: Use the pronouns that take the topic slot
points.explanation: The ang set replaces an ang phrase: ako 'I', ka/ikaw 'you', siya 'he/she', kami 'we (not you)', tayo 'we (including you)', kayo 'you (pl/polite)', sila 'they'. ka goes after the verb, ikaw goes first. Tagalog splits 'we' the way Indonesian does — kami excludes the listener, tayo includes them.

drills.hint: the ang-set pronoun for the speaker, sitting right after the verb
the short second-person topic pronoun, the one that leans on the word before it and can never open the sentence
the ang-set pronoun for a single other person — gender is not marked

drills.translation: We (you and I) will go to Baguio tomorrow.
drills.hint: the ang-set 'we' that counts the listener in
the ang-set pronoun for a group of other people
the ang-set pronoun for more than one person you are speaking to

drills.translation: We (not you) weren't at home yesterday.
drills.hint: the ang-set 'we' that shuts the listener out

points.title: ng pronouns
points.function: Say who did it when the object is the topic
points.explanation: The ng set marks a non-topic actor or a possessor: ko 'I/my', mo 'you/your', niya 'he/his, she/her', namin 'our (excl)', natin 'our (incl)', ninyo 'your (pl)', nila 'their'. In object-focus sentences the actor is always a ng pronoun: Kinain KO ang mansanas. As possessors they follow the noun: bahay ko 'my house'.

drills.hint: the ng-set actor for the speaker, since the apple is what the sentence is about
the ng-set actor for one other person, while the book holds the topic slot
the possessor pronoun that follows the noun, 'our' with the listener left out
the ng-set actor for a single person you are speaking to
the ng-set actor for several other people

drills.translation: Let's (you and I) finish this before we go home.
drills.hint: the ng-set actor for 'we' with the listener counted in — the work is shared

drills.translation: Where are your children? (asking both parents)
drills.hint: the possessor pronoun placed after the noun, for more than one owner you are addressing

points.title: sa pronouns and possession
points.function: Say to me, for you, and mine
points.explanation: The sa set marks a location, recipient, or emphatic possessor: akin 'me/mine', iyo 'you/yours', kaniya 'him/her/theirs', amin, atin, inyo, kanila. With sa they give direction (sa akin 'to me'); alone and fronted they possess emphatically (Akin ang bahay 'The house is MINE'). Everyday possession still uses the ng set after the noun.

drills.hint: the sa-set pronoun for the speaker as the one receiving
fronted — emphatic possession
the sa-set pronoun for several other people, marked as the recipients
the sa-set pronoun standing alone as the predicate — ownership by more than one other person
the sa-set pronoun for the single person you are speaking to, fronted for emphasis
the sa-set pronoun for one other person, here saying who the book is with

drills.sentence: Pupunta kami sa {{answer}} bukas ng hapon.
drills.translation: We'll come over to your place (yours and your family's) tomorrow afternoon.
drills.hint: the sa-set pronoun standing for the home of the people you are addressing

points.title: si and sina: names take their own marker
points.function: Mark people's names correctly
points.explanation: Personal names never take ang. They take si (singular) and sina (plural) in the topic slot, ni/nina as non-topic actor or possessor, and kay/kina after sa. Using ang with a name is one of the most audible learner errors: *ang Maria is simply wrong; si Maria is right.

drills.hint: a personal name takes its own topic marker instead of the ordinary one — one person here
the name marker for a non-topic actor, doing the job the ng phrase would do for a common noun
the name marker used where sa would stand before an ordinary noun
the topic marker for names in the shape used when two people arrive together

drills.sentence: Nasira ang kotse {{answer}} Ana at Lito.
drills.translation: Ana and Lito's car broke down.
drills.hint: the non-topic name marker in its plural shape, marking who owns the car
drills.gloss: PFV-break · NOM · car · ___ · Ana · and · Lito

drills.sentence: Pumunta kami {{answer}} Lola at Lolo noong Pasko.
drills.translation: We went to Grandma and Grandpa's place at Christmas.
drills.hint: the sa-form name marker in its plural shape — the household they visited
drills.gloss: go.PFV.ACT · 1PL.EXCL.NOM · ___ · grandmother · and · grandfather · PST-LINK · Christmas

drills.hint: even after the negator, a personal name needs the marker reserved for names, never the ordinary topic marker

points.title: Questions: ba and the question words
points.function: Ask yes/no and wh- questions
points.explanation: ba turns any statement into a yes/no question and sits after the first word or phrase: Kumain ka ba? Question words come first and are usually followed by ang or a linker: ano 'what', sino 'who', saan 'where', kailan 'when', bakit 'why', paano 'how', magkano 'how much', ilan 'how many'.

drills.hint: the particle that makes this a yes/no question rather than a statement
the question word for a thing or a name, followed by the topic marker
the question word for place, the one used with a verb rather than for locating a thing
the question word that asks for a reason
the question word that asks which person did it

drills.translation: When did you all arrive in Manila?
drills.hint: the question word that asks for a time

drills.sentence: {{answer}} po ang isang kilo ng bigas?
drills.translation: How much is a kilo of rice? (polite)
drills.hint: the question word that asks a price
drills.gloss: ___ · POL · NOM · one-LINK · kilo · GEN · rice

points.title: ma- adjectives and the linker
points.function: Describe things and attach the description
points.explanation: Most descriptive words take ma-: maganda 'beautiful', mabait 'kind', malaki 'big', mabilis 'fast'. To attach one to a noun you need the linker: -ng after a vowel (magandang bahay), na after a consonant (bahay na maganda). Either order works — what is not optional is the linker.

drills.translation: They live in a beautiful house.
drills.hint: maganda + -ng linker
the linker written as its own word rather than glued to the word before it
a ma- adjective in the predicate slot, first in the sentence, so nothing links it to the topic
mabilis + na linker
the linker in its suffixed shape, welded onto a host that ends in a vowel

drills.sentence: Naghahanap ako ng bahay {{answer}} malapit sa paaralan.
drills.translation: I'm looking for a house near the school.
drills.hint: the standalone linker, required here because the noun before it ends in a consonant
drills.gloss: search.PROG · 1SG.NOM · GEN · house · ___ · ADJ-near · LOC · school

drills.translation: Is the water from the tap cold?
drills.hint: a ma- adjective about temperature, standing as the predicate before the question particle

points.title: i- focus: benefactive and instrument
points.function: Make the thing given, or the tool, the topic
points.explanation: i- puts the thing transferred, the beneficiary's object, or the instrument in the topic slot: Ibinigay ko ang libro 'I gave the book'; Ipinambili ko ang pera 'I used the money to buy'. Compare the three: Binigyan ko ang bata (the CHILD is topic, -an) vs Ibinigay ko ang libro (the BOOK is topic, i-).

drills.hint: i- + bigay — the book is the topic

drills.translation: He used the new knife to cut.
drills.hint: ipang- — instrument focus
i- + dala, contemplated

drills.translation: I threw out the rubbish earlier.
drills.hint: i- + tapon, completed

points.title: ma- and maka-: ability and the involuntary
points.function: Say could, managed to, and happened to
points.explanation: ma- and maka- mark ability or an unintended action: nakita ko 'I saw / happened to see' (versus tiningnan ko 'I looked at'); narinig 'heard' vs pinakinggan 'listened to'; nakapunta 'managed to go'. Perception verbs live almost entirely in this set — you rarely 'deliberately see'.

drills.hint: ma- + kita — perception, not deliberate

drills.translation: I didn't hear what you said.
drills.hint: ma- + rinig

drills.sentence: {{answer}} ako sa Maynila noong isang taon.
drills.translation: I managed to go to Manila last year.
drills.hint: maka- + punta — ability
maka- + pasa, negated

points.title: Enclitic particles and their order
points.function: Place na, pa, ba, po and daw correctly
points.explanation: Tagalog has a set of little words that cling after the first stressed word, in a fixed order: na 'already/now', pa 'still/yet', ba (question), po/ho (respect), daw/raw 'reportedly', naman (contrast/softener), kasi 'because', nga 'indeed'. Kumain na ba kayo? Getting the ORDER wrong is what marks a learner more than any single word choice.

drills.hint: the completion clitic, 'by now'; it has to sit ahead of the question clitic
with hindi it means 'not yet'; the one-syllable clitic for something still outstanding, the opposite of the completion one
the respect marker used to an elder or a stranger; the fuller of the two deferential clitics

drills.translation: The weather is nice, they say.
drills.hint: reportedly — you are relaying what other people say, not what you saw yourself; the d-spelling is the one wanted here, though after a vowel-final word careful writing prefers its r-twin

drills.translation: I'll be the one to pay this time.
drills.hint: the softening clitic that flips whose turn it is: this time it is on me, not on you

drills.translation: The class is over now (said respectfully).
drills.hint: two clitics in one slot, in the fixed order: the completion one first, then the fuller of the two respect words

drills.sentence: Masakit {{answer}} ang ulo ko, kaya hindi ako pumasok.
drills.translation: My head hurt, you see, so I didn't go in.
drills.hint: the clitic that supplies the reason, clinging right after the first word of its own clause
drills.gloss: ADJ-pain · ___ · NOM · head · 1SG.GEN · so · NEG · 1SG.NOM · enter.PFV

points.title: ay inversion
points.function: Write the formal, subject-first order
points.explanation: Default Tagalog is predicate-first: Maganda ang bahay. Fronting the topic requires the marker ay: Ang bahay ay maganda. This is the register of writing, speeches and formal instruction — everyday speech uses it sparingly. In writing ay is often contracted to 'y after a vowel: Ako'y masaya.

drills.hint: topic first, description second: the formal order needs its marker in the middle
a fronted name before a noun predicate; the written, speech-giving register needs its marker here
the pronoun ends in a vowel, so in careful writing the marker contracts onto it
a plural topic fronted before an incompleted verb; the inversion marker still goes in between
fronted topic with a negated predicate; the formal marker still has to stand between them
the fronted phrase ends in a vowel, so in writing the marker shrinks and hooks onto it
a time expression has been pulled to the front; formal Filipino puts the same inversion marker after it

points.title: Comparison: mas, kaysa, pinaka-
points.function: Say more, than, and most
points.explanation: mas X (kaysa sa Y) is 'more X than Y': Mas mataas siya kaysa sa akin. The superlative is pinaka-: pinakamaganda 'most beautiful', pinakamalaki 'biggest'. Equality uses kasing-/sing-: kasingtaas 'as tall as'. mas is a Spanish loan and is now completely standard.

drills.hint: the little comparative word that stands in front of the adjective and pairs with kaysa sa — neither the equality prefix nor the superlative one

drills.translation: She is the smartest in the class.
drills.hint: pinaka- + matalino

drills.translation: He is as tall as me.
drills.hint: kasing- — equality

drills.translation: This is the biggest house on the street.
drills.hint: pinaka- + malaki

drills.sentence: Mas gusto ko ang kape {{answer}} sa tsaa.
drills.hint: the word that introduces what the coffee is measured against; it comes directly before sa
drills.gloss: more · want · 1SG.GEN · NOM · coffee · ___ · DAT · tea

points.title: Pseudo-verbs: gusto, ayaw, dapat, puwede
points.function: Say want, don't want, should, may
points.explanation: These take no aspect of their own and are followed by a ng pronoun plus a verb: Gusto kong kumain 'I want to eat' (note the linker -ng on gusto). ayaw 'not want', kailangan 'need', dapat 'should', puwede/maaari 'may, can', kaya 'be able'. With a noun they take the ng set directly: Gusto ko ng kape.

drills.hint: desire, not need and not permission; the linker rides on the ng-pronoun that follows
refusal: the built-in negative of wanting, so no hindi is needed in front of it
obligation — what one ought to do, out of duty rather than circumstance; not a wish, and not a request for permission
permission rather than ability; the everyday Spanish-derived one, not its formal native twin

drills.translation: They need to leave early tomorrow.
drills.hint: necessity imposed by circumstance rather than by duty; still a pseudo-verb, so it carries no aspect of its own

drills.translation: We (not you) want to sleep early.
drills.hint: the ng-set 'we' that shuts the listener out, with the linker fused onto its end

drills.sentence: {{answer}} mo ba itong gawin nang mag-isa?
drills.translation: Can you manage to do this on your own?
drills.hint: capability: you are asking whether they are up to it, not whether they are allowed

points.title: may and mayroon
points.function: Say there is, and have
points.explanation: may goes straight before the thing (May aso ako 'I have a dog'); mayroon/meron is used when a pronoun or particle comes between (Mayroon akong aso), and stands alone as an answer (Mayroon! 'There is!'). The negative for both is wala.

drills.hint: possession stated with the noun straight after it: the short form is the one that admits nothing in between
the longer existence form, forced here because the pronoun comes before the thing owned; give it in full, not the clipped everyday spelling
the negative that answers both existence words; the pronoun leans on it with a linker
the longer form again: the yes-no question particle sits between it and the noun, and it is the full spelling that is wanted, not the clipped everyday one

drills.translation: There's a new store on the corner.
drills.hint: nobody owns anything here, it is plain existence; use the short word that sits directly before the noun phrase
the one negative word that covers both 'there isn't' and 'doesn't have', with the listener's pronoun leaning on it

drills.translation: Is there any coffee left? — There is!
drills.hint: as a one-word reply nothing follows it, so the short form that must lean on a noun is impossible; give the full written form rather than its clipped everyday variant

points.title: Counting: native and Spanish numbers
points.function: Use the right number system for the job
points.explanation: Tagalog keeps two sets. Native (isa, dalawa, tatlo…) is used for counting things, ages and general quantity. Spanish-derived (uno, dos, tres…, and singko, diyes, bente) dominates time, money and prices — alas-dos 'two o'clock', bente pesos. Using native numbers for money sounds odd; using Spanish ones for 'three children' sounds odd too.

drills.hint: native + linker — counting people
Spanish — telling time
Spanish — money
native + linker

drills.sentence: {{answer}} na taong gulang ang bunso ko.
drills.translation: My youngest is six years old.
drills.hint: ages are counted with the native set, never the Spanish one; the English gives you the value

drills.sentence: Nagbayad ako ng {{answer}} piso para sa pamasahe.
drills.translation: I paid twenty pesos for the fare.
drills.hint: fares and prices reach for the Spanish-derived set; the number itself is in the English
drills.gloss: PFV-pay · 1SG · GEN · ___ · peso · for · LOC · fare

drills.translation: Are four of you going to the wedding?
drills.hint: counting people takes the native set even inside a question; the English supplies the figure

points.title: Deictics: ito, iyan, iyon
points.function: Point at things by distance from the speaker
points.explanation: Three degrees, not two: ito 'this (near me)', iyan 'that (near you)', iyon 'that (far from both)'. They inflect like ang-phrases — nito/niyan/niyon for the ng set, dito/diyan/doon for place. The three-way split maps onto the speaker/listener/elsewhere distinction, not simple distance.

drills.hint: the demonstrative for what the speaker is holding or can touch
the demonstrative for the thing over by the person being spoken to
the place form for somewhere away from speaker and listener alike

drills.translation: The price of this is high.
drills.hint: the ng-set form of the near-speaker demonstrative, marking what the price belongs to

drills.translation: That one over there is my grandmother's house.
drills.hint: the third degree of the set: the house is away from the speaker and away from the listener as well

drills.sentence: Halika {{answer}}, may ipapakita ako sa iyo.
drills.translation: Come here, I have something to show you.
drills.hint: the place form matching the near-speaker demonstrative; the speaker is calling someone over to their own spot

drills.translation: What are you doing there (where you are)?
drills.hint: the place form for where the listener is standing, not the speaker's spot and not somewhere off beyond them both

points.title: Causatives: magpa- and pa-...-in
points.function: Say you had someone do something
points.explanation: magpa- makes the causer the topic (Nagpaluto ako ng pagkain 'I had food cooked'); pa-...-in makes the person made to act the topic (Pinaluto ko siya 'I made him cook'); ipa- makes the thing the topic (Ipinaluto ko ang isda). Filipino uses causatives where English says 'have someone do' or 'get something done', and it is far more frequent than the English equivalent.

drills.hint: magpa- + gawa — the causer is topic
pa-...-in — the cook is topic

drills.translation: I had the clothes washed by the laundrywoman.
drills.hint: ipa- — the clothes are topic

drills.translation: He had himself examined by a doctor.
drills.hint: magpa- + tingin

points.title: Recent perfective: ka- + reduplication
points.function: Say something has only just happened
points.explanation: A distinct aspect English has no single form for: ka- plus reduplication of the first syllable means the action finished a moment ago. Kakakain ko lang 'I just ate'; Kararating lang niya 'He's only just arrived'. It is almost always accompanied by lang. Learners tend to reach for the completed aspect and lose the 'just now' that Tagalog states outright.

drills.hint: ka- + reduplication — recent perfective
ka- + rating
ka- + linis
ka- + panood

points.title: Nominalisation: pag-, pagka-, ka-...-an
points.function: Turn actions and qualities into nouns
points.explanation: pag- + root names the act (pagkain 'eating, food', pag-aaral 'studying'); pagka- names the manner or the state of having done it (pagkakain 'the way of eating', pagkatapos 'after'); ka-...-an names abstractions (kaganda-han 'beauty', kalayaan 'freedom', kabaitan 'kindness'). Formal Filipino writing is built from these.

drills.hint: pag- + reduplicated aral
ka-...-an from laya
pagka- + tapos

drills.translation: She is known for her kindness.
drills.hint: ka-...-an from bait

points.title: Relative clauses with na and -ng
points.function: Attach a whole clause to a noun
points.explanation: The same linker that joins an adjective joins a clause: ang taong kumain 'the person who ate', ang librong binasa ko 'the book that I read'. The verb inside the clause must be in the focus that makes the head noun its topic — you cannot say *ang librong bumasa ako, because bumasa makes the READER the topic. Focus and relativisation are locked together.

drills.hint: the host word ends in a vowel, so the linker attaches to it as a suffix instead of standing free

drills.sentence: Ang libro{{answer}} binasa ko ay maganda.
drills.translation: The book I read is good.
drills.hint: object focus inside the clause

drills.sentence: Ang bahay {{answer}} tinitirhan nila ay malaki.
drills.translation: The house they live in is big.
drills.hint: the host word ends in a consonant, so the linker cannot attach — it stays a separate word

drills.sentence: Ang babae{{answer}} nagluto ay nanay ko.
drills.translation: The woman who cooked is my mother.
drills.hint: actor focus — she is the topic

drills.translation: The food that Grandma cooked is delicious.
drills.hint: the head noun is the thing cooked, so the clause verb must be the form that makes it the topic — root luto, completed

drills.sentence: Kilala mo ba ang lalaking {{answer}} kanina?
drills.translation: Do you know the man who called earlier?
drills.hint: he is the one doing it, so the clause verb takes the actor-focus infix on tawag, completed

drills.sentence: Ang tindahang {{answer}} namin kahapon ay sarado na.
drills.translation: The store we went to yesterday is already closed.
drills.hint: the head noun is the destination, not the goer, so the clause verb has to be the locative focus of punta, completed
drills.gloss: NOM · store-REL · ___ · 1PL.GEN · yesterday · TOP · closed · already

points.title: Conditionals: kung, kapag, sana
points.function: Say if, when, and if only
points.explanation: kung is 'if' for uncertain conditions and also 'whether'; kapag/pag is 'when(ever)' for things expected to happen. sana carries the wish or counterfactual: Sana umulan 'I hope it rains'; Kung mayaman ako, sana… 'If I were rich…'. Tagalog puts the unreality in sana, not in the verb.

drills.translation: If it rains, I won't go.
drills.hint: an uncertain condition — the rain may or may not come, so the doubtful conjunction is the one that fits

drills.translation: Whenever I go home, I call.
drills.hint: the conjunction for something expected to recur, every single time, rather than a doubtful possibility — and the full two-syllable form of it, not the clipped one
the particle that carries the wish; Tagalog marks the unreality here rather than on the verb

drills.translation: I don't know whether he'll come.
drills.hint: after 'I don't know', this conjunction introduces an embedded yes-or-no question

drills.sentence: Kung nandito ka kahapon, hindi {{answer}} ako naligaw.
drills.translation: If you had been here yesterday, I wouldn't have gotten lost.
drills.hint: the unreality particle for a past that did not happen, sitting right after the negator

drills.sentence: Ano ang gagawin natin {{answer}} hindi dumating ang bus?
drills.translation: What will we do if the bus doesn't come?
drills.hint: the bus failing to arrive is only a possibility, not an expectation — the doubtful conjunction, here inside a question
drills.gloss: what · NOM · do.FUT.OBJ · 1PL.GEN · ___ · NEG · come.INF · NOM · bus

drills.sentence: {{answer}} tapos na ang klase, umuwi ka agad.
drills.translation: When class is over, go home right away.
drills.hint: the clipped everyday form of the 'when(ever)' conjunction, one syllable shorter than the full one
drills.gloss: ___ · finished · already · NOM · class · go.home.IMP · 2SG · immediately

points.title: Reciprocal and social affixes
points.function: Say to each other, and to go along with
points.explanation: mag-...-an makes an action mutual: magkita 'meet each other', magtulungan 'help one another', mag-usap 'talk to each other'. makipag- means joining in with someone: makipag-usap 'converse with', makipaglaro 'play with'. These carry the social texture of Filipino, where doing things together is grammatically marked rather than just implied.

drills.hint: mag- reciprocal

drills.translation: They helped one another during the storm.
drills.hint: mag-...-an

drills.translation: I want to talk with him.
drills.hint: makipag- — joining in

drills.translation: The children are playing with each other.
drills.hint: mag-...-an, incompleted

drills.sentence: {{answer}} siya sa mga pinsan niya kahapon.
drills.translation: She played with her cousins yesterday.
drills.hint: the 'join in with someone' prefix on laro, completed — she went along with a game already going

drills.translation: When will we see each other again?
drills.hint: the mutual 'seeing' verb built on kita, contemplated — the root's first syllable doubles
root mahal in the mutual pattern, prefix and suffix together, in the plain form a modal takes

points.title: pang- instruments and other noun prefixes
points.function: Name the tool and the season
points.explanation: pang- (pam-/pan- by the same nasal rule as Indonesian's meN-) names an instrument: panulat 'writing tool', pambura 'eraser', panghiwa 'cutter'. tag- names a season or period: tag-ulan 'rainy season', tag-init 'hot season', taglamig 'cold season'. ka- names a partner or counterpart: kaibigan 'friend', kapatid 'sibling', katrabaho 'workmate'.

drills.translation: The pen is on the table.
drills.hint: pang- + sulat — instrument

drills.translation: The rain is heavy during the rainy season.
drills.hint: the season prefix on the word for rain — a vowel-initial root keeps the hyphen

drills.translation: He is my workmate at the office.
drills.hint: the counterpart prefix, the same one behind the words for friend and sibling, on the ordinary word for work
pang- → pam- before b

drills.sentence: Bumili ako ng {{answer}} para sa proyekto ko.
drills.translation: I bought glue for my project.
drills.hint: an instrument noun from the root meaning 'to stick' — the nasal prefix shows up in its n form here

drills.sentence: Mas gusto ko ang {{answer}} kaysa sa tag-ulan.
drills.translation: I prefer the cold season to the rainy season.
drills.hint: the season prefix on the word for cold — a consonant-initial root takes it with no hyphen
drills.gloss: more · like · 1SG.GEN · NOM · ___ · than · LOC · SEASON-rain

drills.translation: Who lives with you at home?
drills.hint: the counterpart prefix on the root meaning 'to go along' — the one who shares the house with you

points.title: Register: Filipino, deep Tagalog, and Taglish
points.function: Move between the three registers educated speakers use
points.explanation: Three registers coexist. Formal Filipino (news, school) prefers ay-inversion and native coinages. Deep or 'malalim' Tagalog uses words most urban speakers now find literary — salumpuwit for upuan, and the older particles. Taglish mixes English freely (Nag-aral ako ng math kanina) and is the everyday register of Metro Manila, including among the highly educated. Choosing wrongly is what marks a foreigner long after the grammar is right.

drills.translation: The child is diligent in studying.
drills.hint: the inversion particle of formal written Filipino, standing between the fronted topic and the comment about it
Taglish — English noun in Tagalog frame
polite register with po
Taglish verbalisation of an English noun

drills.sentence: Umulan nang malakas kagabi, {{answer}} nagpatuloy pa rin ang laro.
drills.translation: It rained hard last night, but the game still went on.
drills.hint: the contrastive conjunction of news and classroom Filipino; the everyday spoken one is a Spanish loan
drills.gloss: rain.PFV.ACT · LNK · ADJ-strength · PST-night · ___ · continue.PFV.ACT · still · also · NOM · game

drills.hint: politeness reaches for the plural ang-pronoun even though one elder is being addressed

points.title: Focus choice as information structure
points.function: Pick the focus that puts the right thing in view
points.explanation: Focus is not style — it decides what the sentence is ABOUT and which noun is definite. Bumili ako ng libro 'I bought a book' (indefinite book, actor in view); Binili ko ang libro 'I bought the book' (definite book, the book in view). A definite object nearly forces object focus. This is the deepest difference from European languages and the last thing learners get right.

drills.translation: I bought a book at the store.
drills.hint: actor focus — the book is indefinite
object focus — the book is definite
-an — the recipient is in view

drills.translation: He gave the money to the child.
drills.hint: i- — the money is in view

drills.sentence: Ano ang {{answer}} mo sa kaniya kagabi?
drills.translation: What did you say to him last night?
drills.hint: the questioned thing is what the sentence is about, so the verb must put it in topic — root sabi, completed

drills.sentence: {{answer}} muna ako ng tanghalian bago umalis.
drills.translation: I'll eat lunch first before leaving.
drills.hint: no particular meal is in view, so the eater stays the topic — root kain, contemplated

drills.translation: I haven't taken the medicine yet.
drills.hint: a specific, already-known medicine is what the sentence is about — root inom, completed, object in topic

points.title: Aspect subtleties: na, pa, and the contemplated
points.function: Say already, still, and not-yet precisely
points.explanation: na and pa do work the verb form alone cannot. Kumakain pa siya 'He's still eating' vs Kumain na siya 'He has eaten'. Hindi pa 'not yet' contrasts with hindi 'not at all'. With the contemplated aspect, na means 'now, at last': Aalis na ako 'I'm leaving now'. Aspect plus particle is one system, and translating each half separately produces sentences that are grammatical and wrong.

drills.hint: the eating is unfinished; the enclitic for an action still under way
the enclitic that marks the meal as over and its result as current
after hindi, the enclitic that makes the sleeping merely not started yet, rather than refused outright
with a contemplated verb, the enclitic that reads ‘now, at last’ instead of pushing the departure further off
the hunger has not ended; the continuing-state enclitic goes ahead of the yes/no marker

drills.translation: I don't have any money left.
drills.hint: with an existential, the enclitic saying the money ran out at some point and has stayed gone

drills.translation: I'm not going home until later.
drills.hint: with a contemplated verb, the enclitic that pushes the event off, ruling out anything before the stated time

points.title: Literary and formal Filipino
points.function: Read the register of literature and official texts
points.explanation: Literary Filipino keeps forms that everyday speech has shed: ay-inversion throughout, nga and kay as intensifiers (Kay ganda! 'How beautiful!'), ani 'said', the older -in- infix placements, and native coinages minted to replace Spanish and English loans. National literature, the constitution and formal oratory all live here, and none of it sounds like the street.

drills.hint: the literary exclamative that fronts a bare adjective root to mean ‘how …!’, where speech would use ang ganda
the literary quotative for ‘said’ after a quotation in narrative prose, where ordinary speech uses sabi
the inversion marker standing between a fronted topic and its predicate; formal prose keeps it where speech drops it
the affirming enclitic that adds ‘indeed’ to a formal declaration

drills.sentence: Nagtitipon tayo ngayon {{answer}} mahalaga ang araw na ito.
drills.translation: We gather today because this day is important.
drills.hint: the formal causal conjunction of oratory and legal prose, where conversation would simply say kasi
drills.gloss: gather.IPFV.ACT · 1PL.INCL.NOM · now · ___ · important · NOM · day · LNK · this

drills.sentence: Ang {{answer}} ay may tungkuling maglingkod sa mamamayan.
drills.translation: The government has a duty to serve the people.
drills.hint: the native coinage for the governing body; official and constitutional Filipino avoids the Spanish loan gobyerno
drills.gloss: NOM · ___ · INV · EXIST · duty-LNK · serve.INF.ACT · OBL · citizen

drills.hint: the literary optative enclitic that turns a plain statement into a wish, as in blessings and oratory

points.title: Lexicalised affixation
points.function: Recognise affixed words that have left their roots behind
points.explanation: Many affixed Tagalog words no longer mean the sum of their parts. kapatid 'sibling' is not a live ka- + patid; pagkain means 'food', not only 'the act of eating'; magulang 'parent' has drifted from ulang; kasama can be 'companion' or 'included' depending on context. Decomposing these confidently is the reliable way to be wrong.

drills.hint: the everyday noun for a brother or sister; it looks like a ka- form, but the parts no longer add up to the meaning
the pag- noun that has settled into meaning what is on the plate, not the activity itself

drills.translation: Tax is included in the price.
drills.hint: kasama — 'included' here
the noun for a mother or father; mga does the pluralising here, and the apparent root no longer explains the meaning

drills.sentence: Hindi ko siya {{answer}}; katrabaho ko lang siya.
drills.translation: He isn't my friend; he's just a co-worker of mine.
drills.hint: unlike katrabaho beside it, this one is lexicalised: it names a person you are close to, not a shared act of liking
a ka-…-an noun for the physical self; the syllables left after the prefix are not a word you could look up

points.title: Code-switching as a system
points.function: Switch languages mid-sentence the way bilinguals do
points.explanation: Taglish is rule-governed, not random. English content words slot into Tagalog frames with Tagalog affixes (nag-drive, i-check, na-stress), while the grammatical skeleton — markers, pronouns, aspect, particles — stays Tagalog. The switch tracks topic and formality: technical and professional material tilts English, feeling and family tilt Tagalog, often inside one sentence. Producing this naturally is the final register skill.

drills.hint: the focus prefix used for things handed over, here on an English root
actor focus, completed aspect, on an English root: the prefix that replaces mag- once the action has happened
ma- involuntary, completed
the conveyance focus prefix again, on the English root following a pseudo-verb of permission

drills.sentence: {{answer}}-deliver ko ang cake sa office niya.
drills.translation: I had the cake delivered to her office.
drills.hint: causative on an English root, completed and object focus: you did not do it yourself, you got someone else to
